q: Change the following sentence into Passive Voice: The gardener waters the plants every morning.
o: The plants were watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants have been watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants are being watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.
e: Present Simple Active ("waters") changes to Passive using "is/am/are + V3" ("are watered"). Plural subject "The plants" takes "are".

q: Convert into Passive Voice: She was writing a letter when I entered.
o: A letter was written by her when I entered.
A letter is being written by her when I entered.
A letter had been written by her when I entered.
A letter was being written by her when I entered.
e: Past Continuous Active ("was writing") converts to Passive using "was/were + being + V3" ("was being written"). The subordinate clause ("when I entered") stays unchanged.

q: Change into Passive Voice: Open the door immediately.
o: You are requested to open the door immediately.
The door should be opening immediately.
Let the door opened immediately.
Let the door be opened immediately.
e: Transitive imperative commands ("V1 + Object") take the Passive structure "Let + Object + be + V3" ("Let the door be opened immediately").

q: Convert into Passive Voice: We must obey the traffic rules.
o: The traffic rules must obeyed by us.
The traffic rules are obeyed by us.
The traffic rules ought to be obeyed by us.
The traffic rules must be obeyed.
e: Modal verbs ("can, may, must, should, will") form the Passive with "modal + be + V3" ("must be obeyed"). Vague/general agents like "by us" are commonly omitted.

q: Transform into Comparative Degree without changing meaning: Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.
o: Mount Everest is higher than all other peaks in the world.
Mount Everest is higher than any other peak in the world.
Mount Everest is more high than any peak in the world.
No other peak in the world is higher than Mount Everest.
e: Superlative ("the + est") transforms to Comparative using "comparative + than any other + singular noun" ("higher than any other peak"). Note: "any other" must be followed by a singular noun, while "all other" takes a plural noun; option B is the canonical singular UP TGT form.

q: Change into Comparative Degree: Rahul is as tall as Vivek.
o: Vivek is taller than Rahul.
Vivek is less tall than Rahul.
Rahul is taller than Vivek.
Vivek is not taller than Rahul.
e: An affirmative Positive equality ("A is as + adj + as B") becomes a negative Comparative ("B is not + comparative + than A"): "Vivek is not taller than Rahul."

q: Remove "too" without changing the meaning: He is too weak to walk.
o: He is so weak to walk.
He is so weak that he could not walk.
He is very weak to walk.
He is so weak that he cannot walk.
e: "too + adjective + to + V1" in the present tense transforms into "so + adjective + that + subject + cannot + V1". Hence, "He is so weak that he cannot walk."

q: Transform into a Negative sentence without altering the meaning: Everybody loves his motherland.
o: Nobody loves his motherland.
Nobody does not love his motherland.
Everybody does not hate his motherland.
There is nobody who does not love his motherland.
e: Universal affirmative "Everybody + V1" transforms cleanly into negative via "There is nobody who does not + V1" (or "Nobody hates his motherland").

q: Transform into an Interrogative sentence without changing meaning: Everyone knows Mahatma Gandhi.
o: Does everyone know Mahatma Gandhi?
Did everyone know Mahatma Gandhi?
Who knows Mahatma Gandhi?
Who does not know Mahatma Gandhi?
e: An affirmative statement starting with "Everyone / Everybody" converts to a rhetorical Interrogative using "Who does not + V1...?", which implies "Everyone does".

q: Transform into an Assertive sentence: How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank!
o: The moonlight sleeps sweetly upon this bank.
Does the moonlight sleep sweetly upon this bank?
The moonlight is very sweet upon this bank.
The moonlight sleeps very sweetly upon this bank.
e: In exclamatory-to-assertive conversion, "How + adverb/adjective" is replaced by "very + adverb/adjective" in normal subject-verb order ("sleeps very sweetly").

q: Transform into a Compound sentence: Seeing a tiger, the traveller climbed a tree.
o: The traveller saw a tiger and climbed a tree.
When the traveller saw a tiger, he climbed a tree.
Because the traveller saw a tiger, he climbed a tree.
Having seen a tiger, the traveller climbed a tree.
e: A Compound sentence joins two independent coordinate clauses with a coordinating conjunction ("and, but, or, so, yet"). Options B and C are Complex sentences; D is Simple.

q: Transform into a Complex sentence: He confessed his guilt.
o: He confessed and he was guilty.
He was guilty, so he confessed.
He confessed being guilty.
He confessed that he was guilty.
e: Expanding the noun phrase "his guilt" into a subordinate Noun Clause ("that he was guilty") turns the Simple sentence into a Complex sentence.

q: Transform using "No sooner...than": As soon as the bell rang, the students rushed out.
o: No sooner the bell rang than the students rushed out.
No sooner did the bell rang when the students rushed out.
No sooner had the bell ring than the students rushed out.
No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out.
e: "No sooner" at the start triggers subject-auxiliary inversion ("did the bell ring", using base verb V1) and is strictly paired with "than" (never "when").

q: Change into a Negative sentence without changing meaning: Only the brave deserve the fair.
o: Never the brave deserve the fair.
Nothing but the brave deserve the fair.
Not only the brave deserve the fair.
None but the brave deserve the fair.
e: When "Only" refers to persons, it is replaced by "None but" in Negative transformation ("Nothing but" is used for things, and "not more than" for numbers).

q: Change into Passive Voice: Who wrote "Hamlet"?
o: By whom was "Hamlet" written?
Who was "Hamlet" written by?
By who was "Hamlet" written?
By whom is "Hamlet" written?
e: Interrogative pronoun "Who" (subject) changes to "By whom" in formal Passive Voice, followed by Past Simple auxiliary "was" + subject + V3 ("written").

q: Convert into Passive Voice: The principal gave him a gold medal.
o: A gold medal was given him by the principal.
He had been given a gold medal by the principal.
He was given a gold medal by the principal.
A gold medal is given to him by the principal.
e: Ditransitive verbs ("give, teach, offer, send") have two objects (indirect "him", direct "a gold medal"). Making the personal indirect object the Passive subject ("He was given a gold medal...") is the most idiomatic Passive form, retaining "a gold medal" as the retained object.

q: Change into Passive Voice: The children laughed at the clown.
o: The clown was laughed by the children.
The clown had been laughed at by the children.
The clown was laughed at by the children.
The clown is laughed at by the children.
e: When a verb is combined with a fixed preposition ("laugh at, look after, listen to"), the preposition MUST be retained immediately after the past participle in Passive Voice ("was laughed at by").

q: Convert into Passive Voice: Her polite behaviour surprised everyone.
o: Everyone was surprised by her polite behaviour.
Everyone was surprised with her polite behaviour.
Everyone was surprised at her polite behaviour.
Everyone was surprised to her polite behaviour.
e: Certain verbs of emotion/state take fixed prepositions other than "by" in the Passive: "surprised at", "known to", "pleased with", "contained in", "interested in".

q: Change into Passive Voice: It is time to close the shop.
o: It is time for the shop to be closed.
It is time that the shop should close.
It is time to be closed the shop.
The shop is time to be closed.
e: The idiomatic pattern "It is time + to + V1 + Object" converts into Passive as "It is time + for + Object + to be + V3" ("It is time for the shop to be closed").

q: Convert into Passive Voice: Honey tastes sweet.
o: Honey is tasted sweet.
Sweet is tasted by honey.
Honey is sweet when it is tasted.
Honey was sweet when tasted.
e: Quasi-passive verbs ("taste, smell, feel, read") followed by an adjective complement convert using the structure: "Subject + be + adjective + when (it is) + V3" ("Honey is sweet when it is tasted").

q: Transform into Positive Degree: Shakespeare is one of the greatest dramatists in the world.
o: No other dramatist in the world is as great as Shakespeare.
Some dramatists in the world are at least as great as Shakespeare.
Very few dramatists in the world are as great as Shakespeare.
Most dramatists in the world are not as great as Shakespeare.
e: "One of the + superlative + plural noun" converts to Positive Degree using "Very few + plural noun + plural verb + as + positive + as" ("Very few dramatists ... are as great as Shakespeare").

q: Transform into Comparative Degree: Kalidasa is one of the greatest poets of India.
o: Kalidasa is greater than any other poet of India.
Kalidasa is greater than all other poets of India.
Kalidasa is greater than most other poets of India.
No other poet of India is greater than Kalidasa.
e: "One of the + superlative" converts to Comparative using "comparative + than most other + plural noun" (never "any other", which would falsely claim Kalidasa is the single greatest).

q: Transform into a Simple sentence: Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
o: Uneasy lies the head and it wears a crown.
Uneasy lies the head wearing a crown, so it suffers.
Uneasy lies the crowned head.
The head wears a crown and lies uneasy.
e: Condensing the relative/adjective clause ("that wears a crown") into a single past-participial adjective ("crowned") yields a concise Simple sentence with only one finite verb ("lies").

q: Transform into a Complex sentence: He is poor, yet he is honest.
o: In spite of his poverty, he is honest.
Although he is poor, he is honest.
Being poor, he is honest.
He is both poor and honest.
e: Replacing the coordinating conjunction "yet" with the subordinating conjunction of concession "Although / Though" creates a Complex sentence. (Options A and C are Simple sentences.)

q: Transform into a Simple sentence: He worked hard, but he failed to win the prize.
o: Though he worked hard, he failed to win the prize.
He worked hard, yet he failed to win the prize.
In spite of working hard, he failed to win the prize.
Because he worked hard, he failed to win the prize.
e: Converting the first clause into a prepositional phrase ("In spite of / Despite + gerund/noun") leaves only one finite verb ("failed"), producing a Simple sentence.

q: Transform into a Complex sentence: Without your help, I cannot succeed.
o: Unless you help me, I cannot succeed.
You must help me, or I cannot succeed.
Help me and I will succeed.
Not having your help, I cannot succeed.
e: "Without + noun phrase" converts into a negative conditional Adverb Clause using "Unless + affirmative verb" ("Unless you help me"). Option B is Compound; D is Simple.

q: Remove "too" without changing meaning: The news is too good to be true.
o: The news is so good that it cannot be true.
The news is so good that one cannot believe it.
The news is very good to be true.
The news is so good that it could not be true.
e: When the subject is non-living ("The news") and followed by "to be + adj", "too...to" expands into "so + adj + that + it + cannot be + adj" ("so good that it cannot be true").

q: Transform using "Hardly...when": As soon as we reached the station, the train departed.
o: Hardly had we reached the station than the train departed.
Hardly we had reached the station when the train departed.
Hardly had we reached the station when the train departed.
Hardly did we reached the station when the train departed.
e: "Hardly / Scarcely" requires Past Perfect inversion ("Hardly had we reached") and is strictly paired with "when" (or "before"), NEVER "than".

q: Change into a Negative sentence without changing meaning: Brutus loved Caesar.
o: Brutus did not hate Caesar.
Brutus never loved Caesar.
Brutus was not without love for Caesar.
Did Brutus not love Caesar?
e: "Brutus was not without love for Caesar" preserves the positive intensity of "loved" (whereas "did not hate" weakens it to mere neutrality—a classic Wren & Martin / UP TGT distinction).

q: Transform into an Exclamatory sentence: I wish I had the wings of a dove.
o: Oh, that I had the wings of a dove!
What wings of a dove I have!
How I wish having the wings of a dove!
Alas! I had the wings of a dove!
e: Assertive sentences expressing ardent wishes ("I wish...") convert into Exclamatory sentences using "O that / Oh, that / Would that / If only + subject + past subjunctive!"

q: Identify the type of the underlined subordinate clause: Tell me "where he has hidden the treasure".
o: Adjective Clause
Adverb Clause of Place
Noun Clause
Principal Clause
e: Although introduced by "where", the clause answers "Tell me WHAT?"—acting as the direct object of the transitive verb "tell". Therefore, it is a Noun Clause (not an Adverb Clause of Place).

q: Identify the type of the underlined subordinate clause: This is the house "where my grandfather was born".
o: Noun Clause
Adverb Clause of Place
Adjective (Relative) Clause
Coordinate Clause
e: Here "where my grandfather was born" directly qualifies the antecedent noun "house" (= in which my grandfather was born). Any clause qualifying a noun/pronoun is an Adjective Clause.

q: Convert into Active Voice: The thief has been caught red-handed.
o: Someone caught the thief red-handed.
The police had caught the thief red-handed.
The police have caught the thief red-handed.
The police are catching the thief red-handed.
e: Present Perfect Passive ("has been caught") requires a Present Perfect Active verb ("have caught") with the logically implied agent ("The police").

q: Rewrite using the NOUN form of "succeeded": He succeeded in his attempt.
o: He was successful in his attempt.
He achieved success in his attempt.
He attempted successfully.
He had succeeded in his attempt.
e: The noun form of the verb "succeed" is "success" ("successful" is an adjective, "successfully" is an adverb). "He achieved/gained success in his attempt" preserves exact meaning.

q: Transform into a Complex sentence: Walk fast, or you will miss the train.
o: Walk fast lest you should miss the train.
If you do not walk fast, you will miss the train.
Walking fast, you will not miss the train.
You must walk fast to catch the train.
e: An imperative warning joined by "or" ("Do X, or Y will happen") converts to a Complex conditional sentence: "If you do not walk fast, you will miss the train" (or "Unless you walk fast...").

q: Convert into Passive Voice: People say that he is a spy.
o: It is said by people that he is a spy.
He is said to be a spy.
He was said to be a spy.
That he is a spy is being said.
e: Impersonal reporting verbs ("say, believe, think, know") in "People say that he is..." transform into the elegant personal Passive using "Subject + is/are + V3 + to-infinitive": "He is said to be a spy." ("It is said that he is a spy" is also valid without "by people".)

q: Change into Passive Voice: She made me laugh.
o: I was made laugh by her.
I was made to laugh by her.
I was being made to laugh by her.
I had been made laugh by her.
e: Causative "make" and verbs of perception ("see, hear, watch") take a bare infinitive in Active Voice ("made me laugh"), but MUST take a full "to-infinitive" in Passive Voice ("was made to laugh"). (Exception: "let" retains the bare infinitive.)

q: Convert into Passive Voice: They believe that he stole the painting.
o: He is believed to steal the painting.
He is believed to have stolen the painting.
He was believed to steal the painting.
It is believed that the painting is stolen.
e: Because the reporting verb ("believe") is in Present Simple while the subordinate action ("stole") occurred earlier in the past, the Passive uses the Perfect Infinitive ("to have + V3"): "He is believed to have stolen the painting."

q: Change into Passive Voice: We elected him President of the club.
o: President of the club was elected him by us.
He was elected President of the club.
He was elected as President of the club by us.
President of the club was elected to him.
e: Factitive verbs ("elect, appoint, make, crown, call") take an object ("him") and an object complement ("President"). In Passive, only the personal object becomes the subject, and "as" is NEVER inserted after "elected".

q: Transform into Comparative Degree: Some poets are at least as great as Tennyson.
o: Tennyson is not greater than all other poets.
Tennyson is not greater than some other poets.
Tennyson is greater than most other poets.
No other poet is greater than Tennyson.
e: "Some + plural noun + are at least as + adj + as X" converts to "X is not + comparative + than some other + plural noun" (which is equivalent to "X is not the greatest of all poets").

q: Transform into a Complex sentence using "lest": Walk carefully, otherwise you may fall.
o: Walk carefully lest you should not fall.
Walk carefully lest you should fall.
Walk carefully lest you may fall.
Walk carefully lest you will fall.
e: "Lest" means "for fear that / so that ... not"; it is inherently negative (never add "not") and is strictly followed by the modal "should" (never "may/will").

q: Transform into a Complex sentence: Despite his vast wealth, he is never content.
o: However wealthy he may be, he is never content.
He has vast wealth, yet he is never content.
Having vast wealth, he is never content.
Although his vast wealth, he is never content.
e: "However + adjective + subject + may be" forms a subordinate Adverb Clause of Concession, creating a grammatical Complex sentence. Option B is Compound; C is Simple; D is ungrammatical ("Although" needs a finite clause).

q: Combine into a single Simple sentence using a Nominative Absolute: The sun rose. The fog dispersed.
o: When the sun rose, the fog dispersed.
The sun having risen, the fog dispersed.
The sun rose and the fog dispersed.
Rising the sun, the fog dispersed.
e: When two clauses have DIFFERENT subjects ("the sun" and "the fog") with a cause-effect/time sequence, they are synthesized into one Simple sentence using the Nominative Absolute ("Subject + having + V3"): "The sun having risen, the fog dispersed."

q: Transform into a Negative sentence without changing meaning: Every rose has a thorn.
o: No rose is without a thorn.
There is no rose which has a thorn.
Not every rose has a thorn.
Every rose does not lack a thorn.
e: "Every X has a Y" converts concisely and idiomatically into "There is no X without a Y" / "No X is without a Y" ("No rose is without a thorn").

q: Remove "too" without changing meaning: The coffee is too hot for me to drink.
o: The coffee is so hot that I cannot drink it.
The coffee is so hot that I cannot drink.
The coffee is so hot for me that I could not drink it.
The coffee is very hot so that I cannot drink it.
e: "for me" supplies the subject "I" of the "that"-clause, and because "drink" is transitive, the pronoun object "it" (referring to "the coffee") MUST be supplied at the end ("that I cannot drink it").

q: Transform by omitting "If" without changing meaning: If I had known of your arrival, I would have met you at the airport.
o: Did I know of your arrival, I would have met you at the airport.
Had I known of your arrival, I would have met you at the airport.
Should I have known of your arrival, I would have met you at the airport.
Were I known of your arrival, I would have met you at the airport.
e: In Type-3 Past Perfect conditionals, "If + subject + had + V3" can be inverted by dropping "If" and fronting "Had": "Had I known of your arrival, I would have met you..."

q: Change into Passive Voice: Let him complete the assignment.
o: Let the assignment be completed by him.
The assignment should be let completed by him.
Let him be completed the assignment.
He is let to complete the assignment.
e: Active imperatives beginning with "Let + indirect agent + V1 + direct object" convert into Passive as "Let + direct object + be + V3 + by + indirect agent": "Let the assignment be completed by him."

q: Transform into a Compound sentence: If you search his pockets, you will find the watch.
o: Searching his pockets, you will find the watch.
Search his pockets and you will find the watch.
Unless you search his pockets, you will not find the watch.
You must search his pockets so as to find the watch.
e: An affirmative conditional Complex sentence ("If you do X, Y will happen") converts into a Compound sentence via an imperative clause + "and" + future clause: "Search his pockets and you will find the watch."

q: Transform into Positive Degree without changing meaning: Gold is more precious than any other metal.
o: No other metal is so precious as gold.
Very few metals are as precious as gold.
No metal is as precious as gold.
Other metals are not more precious than gold.
e: "Comparative + than any other + singular noun" transforms to Positive using "No other + singular noun + singular verb + so/as + positive + as". Omitting "other" (Option C) is logically faulty because gold itself is a metal.

q: Transform into a Simple sentence: He not only gave us good advice, but also helped us financially.
o: Besides giving us good advice, he helped us financially.
Though he gave us good advice, he helped us financially.
He gave us good advice and also helped us financially.
Having given us good advice, he also helped us financially, which was kind.
e: Correlative Compound "not only...but also" condenses into a Simple sentence using the preposition "Besides + gerund" ("Besides giving us good advice, he helped us financially"), leaving only one finite verb ("helped").
